The Nok culture was a farming society of central Nigeria known for its terracotta sculptures and for some of the earliest iron working in West Africa south of the Sahara. Recent dating places its beginnings around 1500 BCE, earlier than older charts show, and it lasted until about the start of the common era.

It is named after the village of Nok in southern Kaduna State, where tin miners found the first terracotta head in 1928. Since then hundreds of sites have been found, over a wide area north of where the Niger and Benue rivers meet.

What we know about its people:

  • They grew pearl millet and other crops, and may have come from the Sahara or the Sahel as it dried.
  • From about 900 BCE they made striking clay figures, often life-sized heads with pierced, triangular eyes and elaborate hairstyles. Some show hunters with bows and slings, and one shows two people paddling a dugout canoe.
  • The sculptures seem to have belonged to funerals and ritual.
  • By the middle of the first millennium BCE they were smelting iron, part of the wider story of iron metallurgy in Africa.

Much is still unknown, partly because looting for the art market has destroyed many sites before archaeologists reached them. Why the culture faded is also unclear. Some scholars see links between Nok sculpture and the later art of Ife and other Nigerian traditions, though the gap of centuries makes that hard to prove. Nok is the oldest known tradition of large figure sculpture in sub-Saharan Africa, and it shows that complex societies grew there alongside the spread of Bantu-speaking farmers to the east and south.
